results.title: What is a neocloud, and how does it price GPUs?
highlights:
A neocloud rents Nvidia GPUs and nothing else; CoreWeave's HGX H100 node lists at $6.16 per GPU-hour on-demand, up to 60% cheaper on a multi-year commit. 

 Published 2026.09.10 · The Hardware Desk

...

A neocloud is a cloud provider, such as CoreWeave, Lambda, Nebius or Crusoe, built entirely around renting Nvidia GPUs rather than general-purpose compute; it prices capacity on two tiers, a high hourly on-demand rate for flexibility and a discounted multi-year committed rate, with the gap (CoreWeave's HGX H100 runs $6.16 per GPU-hour on-demand versus up to 60% less reserved) funding the debt used to buy the GPUs in the first place.

...

- ▸ A neocloud is a cloud provider built entirely around GPU rental, a term SemiAnalysis coined on 3 October 2024 to separate CoreWeave-style specialists from AWS, Azure and GCP.
- ▸ CoreWeave's on-demand HGX H100 node lists at $49.24/hour for 8 GPUs, or $6.16 per GPU-hour, versus up to 60% off for a multi-year committed contract.
- ▸ The blended market rate for an H100 SXM was $2.68 per GPU-hour on 2026-08-26 per Ornn Data's index, well under any single neocloud's posted on-demand sticker.
- ▸ CoreWeave's revenue backlog reached $99.4 billion as of 2026-03-31, the contracted demand that lets it borrow against unbuilt data centers to keep expanding.
- ▸ Neocloud spot pricing swings hard: CoreWeave's HGX H100 spot rate is $19.71/hour, 60% below on-demand, because unsold capacity is a sunk cost the moment the GPU is idle.

...

A neocloud is a cloud provider built entirely around renting Nvidia GPUs, nothing else, and it prices that capacity on two tiers: a high hourly rate for anyone who shows up without a commitment, and a discount of up to 60% for anyone willing to sign a multi-year contract. CoreWeave’s on-demand HGX H100 node runs $49.24 an hour for eight GPUs, or $6.16 per GPU-hour, a rate you can read straight off its public pricing page. The skill this post is really teaching is how to read that gap between on-demand and reserved pricing and understand why it exists, because it tells you exactly what a neocloud is betting on and what happens to your bill if that bet goes wrong.

...

A neocloud is a specialist cloud provider, CoreWeave, Lambda, Nebius and Crusoe are the four SemiAnalysis classified as “neocloud giants” in its October 2024 taxonomy, that sells GPU rental almost exclusively instead of the broad service catalog a hyperscaler like AWS or Azure bundles. Pricing runs on two tracks: an on-demand hourly rate priced for flexibility and idle-capacity risk, and a reserved or committed rate discounted against multi-year contracts, up to 60% off on CoreWeave’s own pricing page. A blended market rate sits below either extreme: Ornn Data’s H100 SXM index settled at $2.68 per GPU-hour on 2026-08-26, versus CoreWeave’s $6.16 on-demand sticker for the same chip. The reserved discount exists because a signed, multi-year contract is exactly what lets a neocloud borrow money to buy the GPUs in the first place, so the price you’re quoted is really a reflection of how much certainty you’re giving the provider.

...

That single fact, an idle GPU costs money and an idle GPU earns nothing, explains the whole pricing structure. On-demand rates are set high because that customer is asking for maximum flexibility with zero commitment, so the provider prices in both the option value it’s giving up and the risk that the same hour goes unsold to someone else. Reserved or committed rates are set low because that customer is providing exactly what a lender wants to see: predictable, contracted cash flow over a multi-year term, the kind of backlog that let CoreWeave carry $99.4 billion in signed but not-yet-delivered revenue as of 2026-03-31. Spot pricing sits at the opposite extreme from on-demand: CoreWeave lists spot HGX H100 capacity at $19.71 an hour, 60% below its on-demand rate, because spot is explicitly the leftover capacity a provider would rather sell cheap than leave idle. The underlying Nvidia H100 silicon (What is a GPU?) doesn’t change between these tiers; only the certainty attached to the rental does.

## The numbers

The gap between on-demand and reserved pricing, and between one neocloud’s sticker price and the broader market, is the whole story. CoreWeave’s own pricing page lists three current Nvidia generations, each as an eight-GPU HGX node:

| GPU (8x HGX node) | On-demand, per node | On-demand, per GPU-hour | Spot, per GPU-hour |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 | $49.24/hr | $6.16 | $2.46 |
| H200 | $50.44/hr | $6.31 | $2.62 |
| B200 | $68.80/hr | $8.60 | $4.26 |

Lambda prices per GPU rather than per node: its H100 SXM runs $3.99 to $4.29 per GPU-hour on-demand and its B200 SXM6 runs $6.69 to $6.99, both lower than CoreWeave’s equivalent on-demand figures, which is consistent with Lambda competing on price within the same neocloud-giant tier. Against both of those sits Ornn Data’s blended H100 index, the same number that answers how much does it cost to rent an H100 per hour?, which settled at $2.68 per GPU-hour on 2026-08-26, below every on-demand figure above because the index averages across many providers and contract structures, including the deep reserved discounts that never show up on a public on-demand rate card. CoreWeave doesn’t publish what those reserved rates actually are by term length or volume, only that committed usage saves “up to 60% over on-demand prices,” so the number a given customer pays sits somewhere between that index average and the on-demand ceiling depending entirely on what they’re willing to sign. Underneath all of this, CoreWeave reported $2.078 billion in Q1 2026 revenue and a 56% adjusted EBITDA margin against that $99.4 billion backlog, evidence that the reserved side of the business, not the on-demand sticker, is what actually funds the buildout.

...

The decision a buyer is actually making is how much certainty to trade for price, and the numbers above make that trade explicit rather than a vibe. A short training run, a burst inference workload, or a proof of concept has no business paying reserved rates, since it can’t offer the multi-year commitment that earns the discount, and it should expect to pay close to CoreWeave’s $6.16 on-demand H100 figure or shop Lambda’s lower on-demand rate instead. A sustained production workload, the kind running 24/7 for a year or more, is the workload the reserved discount was built for, and locking in a multi-year term against a specific GPU generation can plausibly get within range of Ornn Data’s $2.68 blended index rate, sometimes lower, depending on volume. Spot capacity is the third lever, and it’s the right call for anything genuinely interruptible: batch inference, checkpointed training, anything that can tolerate a GPU getting reclaimed mid-job in exchange for CoreWeave’s 60%-off spot rate. What a buyer should not do is compare a hyperscaler’s published on-demand price directly to a neocloud’s on-demand price and call it done, because the real comparison a large buyer makes is neocloud reserved pricing against hyperscaler committed-use discounts, and neither side publishes that number without a sales call.

...

The same debt-funded model that makes reserved pricing cheap is also the model’s biggest risk, and it’s a risk the customer inherits indirectly. A neocloud that financed its GPU buildout against a small number of anchor contracts, Microsoft’s roughly two-thirds share of CoreWeave’s historical revenue is the visible example of that concentration, is exposed if any single customer relationship changes, and a smaller or newer neocloud without that scale of backlog carries the same structural risk with far less cushion. On-demand pricing is also not a stable number to plan around: it moves with GPU generation availability and provider-specific demand, so a rate quoted today for an H100 tells you little about what a B200 or the next generation will cost once it’s the scarce SKU, and CoreWeave’s own B200 on-demand rate already runs 40% above its H100 rate per GPU-hour. Reserved pricing has the opposite failure mode: it locks a buyer into a specific GPU generation and term length before newer, faster hardware ships, the same tradeoff behind NVLink vs PCIe: how much does the link matter? when a training cluster outlives the interconnect generation it was built on. A buyer also can’t assume Nvidia is the only option locked into that contract; some neoclouds now offer AMD capacity too, which is the question Nvidia vs AMD for AI: is ROCm ready yet? actually answers, and a multi-year commitment to one vendor’s silicon is itself a bet on that vendor’s software stack staying ahead over the contract’s life. And the published on-demand numbers themselves are the easy part; the actual reserved rate a given customer pays is negotiated, not listed, so any public price comparison between neoclouds is necessarily comparing the least-informative tier of each provider’s pricing.

Neither vendor will sell you an H200 or a B200 at any price, neither offers spot, and neither can be compelled by a US court order to hand over your data. That is the entire European sovereign-GPU market in one paragraph — and if you run inference for EU users, that paragraph is also your shortlist.

results.title: GPU cost depends entirely on who's selling you the chip, not just which chip it is. Marketplace and boutique clouds (I think of Neocloud as a subset) are renting H100s for $1.38–$1.49 … | Mark Newton
highlights:
# GPU cost depends entirely on who's selling you the chip, not just which chip it is.

...

GPU cost depends entirely on who's selling you the chip, not just which chip it is. Marketplace and boutique clouds (I think of Neocloud as a subset) are renting H100s for $1.38–$1.49 per GPU-hour right now. The same card, on-demand at a hyperscaler, runs $11.68–$12.29 per hour — roughly an 8x spread for identical hardware.

That's a signal about what's actually being priced: not the silicon, but everything wrapped around it — commitment terms, SLA guarantees, network proximity to other services, and the simple fact that a hyperscaler doesn't need to compete on GPU price the way a boutique cloud does.

The FOCUS spec exists partly to solve this — normalize billing data so an 8x spread doesn't hide inside vendor-specific line items nobody can compare apples-to-apples. But normalized billing data doesn't tell you which spread is worth paying. That's a judgment call: workload portability, data gravity, and how much operational risk you're willing to carry on a smaller provider, against the raw hourly number.

results.title: GPU Marketplaces Are Cheapest, Until They Aren't | Blog
highlights:
New data center accelerators are different.

...

The original analysis recorded the ten cheapest current on-demand and spot listings for six GPUs across providers on ComputePrices on 12 September 2026. Reserved commitments were excluded. Here, “marketplaces” includes the host marketplaces and aggregators described below; Runpod Community Cloud is included, while Secure Cloud is not.

These counts measure representation among low-price listings, not percentage savings, capacity, or market share. Mixing spot and on-demand also means the table is not a like-for-like comparison of uninterrupted service. The accompanying provider totals describe catalog coverage, not rentable stock.

Marketplace-style providers occupy seven of the cheapest ten positions for RTX 5090 and RTX 4090, four for H200 and A100 SXM, three for H100 SXM, and two for B200.

| GPU | Marketplaces in cheapest ten | Share | Providers with a listing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RTX 5090 | 7/10 | 70% | 14 |
| RTX 4090 | 7/10 | 70% | 18 |
| H200 | 4/10 | 40% | 39 |
| A100 SXM | 4/10 | 40% | 37 |
| H100 SXM | 3/10 | 30% | 48 |
| B200 | 2/10 | 20% | 28 |

Marketplaces dominate the consumer-card results, but account for a minority of the cheapest data center listings. This is a comparison of six GPU models, not evidence that marketplace competitiveness declines with every increase in hardware price.

On consumer cards, marketplaces hold seven of the cheapest ten positions. Salad was the cheapest listing for both the 4090 and 5090 in this snapshot.

On data center cards, marketplaces hold only two to four positions. Those entries include interruptible capacity, aggregators reselling data center supply, and independent hosts. At the B200 tier, neoclouds that own the hardware set the floor. The only marketplace-style providers in the cheapest ten were an aggregator and a spot listing.

| GPU | Marketplace providers in the cheapest ten |
| --- | --- |
| RTX 5090 | Salad, Theta EdgeCloud, Lium, QuickPod, Vast.ai, Spheron, Runpod Community |
| RTX 4090 | Salad, QuickPod, Lium, Vast.ai, Runpod Community, GPU Outlet, Shadeform |
| H100 SXM | Compute Cheap (spot), Lium, GPU Outlet |
| H200 | Compute Cheap (spot), GPU Outlet, Spheron (spot), Lium |
| A100 SXM | GPU Outlet, Vast.ai, Runpod Community, Spheron (spot) |
| B200 | Spheron (spot), GPU Outlet |

> Price floor is not scalable price. A cheapest listing is one machine in one place. It does not tell you what ten, 64, or 256 identical GPUs will cost, or whether they are available at all.

...

- Per GPU or per node? A normalized rate can hide a 4x or 8x minimum rental. ComputePrices shows per-GPU rates, but the provider's checkout total is what matters.
- On-demand or interruptible? Vast interruptible bids, Runpod spot pods, Lium spot, Spheron spot, and Compute Cheap capacity can be reclaimed.
- Which tier? Community, secure, spot, standard, and dedicated tiers are different products. Compare them as such.
- Which machine? Check CPU, RAM, storage, bandwidth, location, and host reliability before assuming two GPUs are equivalent.
- Is it in stock? Some providers expose availability. Others publish catalog prices even when no capacity can be provisioned.
- Can it scale? Confirm the number of identical GPUs, topology, and cluster price before planning around the cheapest row.
- Who sets the price? An aggregator's rate is its own. It may sit above or below the underlying supplier's direct price.

results.title: Why H100 Rental Prices Rose 40% While Token Prices Fell
highlights:
> TL;DR: H100 rental prices rose almost 40% between October 2025 and March 2026, from $1.70 to $2.35 per GPU-hour on one-year contracts, while API token prices kept falling. The cost floor under inference is rising even as the sticker price above it drops, and every self-hosting business case written before that shift is now wrong.

...

The number worth reading is the rental contract. H100 one-year rental pricing rose from a low of $1.70 per GPU-hour in October 2025 to $2.35 by March 2026, close to 40%, and on-demand capacity was described as sold out across all GPU types, with half the providers surveyed unable to quote even 8 nodes of H100s or H200s (SemiAnalysis's H100 rental price index). That is not a market pricing in abundance. That is a market rationing.

...

In the CFO commentary accompanying its second-quarter fiscal 2027 results, filed 26 August 2026, Nvidia disclosed that its supply commitments increased from $119 billion in the prior quarter to $279 billion, "primarily related to the procurement of memory" (Nvidia's Q2 FY2027 CFO commentary, filed with the SEC). The company also said it had partnered with its supplier network "to secure the critical components needed to meet demand for the next several years."

...

What makes this cycle different is that on-demand capacity was reported sold out across all GPU types, with holders refusing to release reserved instances back into the pool despite the price increases. A spot market only offers relief when somebody has spare capacity to sell. When every holder is fully utilised and expects prices to keep rising, the discount disappears at exactly the moment you need it.

...

### Q: How much does an H100 cost to rent per hour?

Published index pricing for one-year H100 contracts was $2.35 per GPU-hour as of March 2026, up from a $1.70 low in October 2025. On-demand and short-term rates sit higher and vary widely by provider and region, and during the 2026 crunch several providers could not quote capacity at any advertised rate. Treat a quoted rate as valid only for the term you can actually sign.

As the AI wave sweeps across the world, high-end GPU compute has become known as the "new oil." Whether for large language model training or inference, rental prices for NVIDIA H100 and B200 GPUs directly affect costs and profitability across the industry. In the past, price discovery for these resources largely took place between institutions and cloud providers, making it difficult for retail traders to participate directly.

Now, Bitget is opening the door. Bitget has officially launched the industry's first pre-market compute perpetuals for retail traders: H100USDT and B200USDT. These futures track the H100 and B200 GPU rental price indices published by Silicon Data. Quoted in USD per GPU hour, the indices reflect standardized average rental costs across multiple cloud service and compute providers. Without purchasing GPUs or renting servers, users can use USDT as margin to go long or short on global AI compute prices. The futures offer up to 10x leverage, 24/7 trading, and funding fee settlements every 8 hours.

This means you can trade the cost of compute itself and participate in price discovery across the global GPU rental and AI infrastructure markets.
